questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I chose Boston because of the language, because I like the city, and because Boston is home to some of the best universities in the world. I was recommended Boston College by a fellow KU student who had been there the previous year.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Being on exchange in Boston was really great. However, the whole process upon studying in the US was very extensive as well as very expensive. It's a lot of work and money for just 4 months abroad.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: I think it was fairly easy to find information about preparation for studying in the US because KU's international team held meetings with us and provided us with an informative powerpoint. It was difficult to find specific information about Boston College though.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: The international team at Boston College was very helpful. They had arranged orientation/introduction days for all the exchange student, and I knew where to find them if I had any questions.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: There were a lot of repetition but it was still helpful.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: Dorms

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: Mandatory meal plan

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about on campus housing? *
questions.answer: Dorm rooms at Boston College are very conveniently located on campus. Close to class rooms and cafeterias. However, you will share a room with at least one other student. You will share bathrooms with the whole floor. The rooms only have basic furniture, so you will have to buy pillows, blankets, desk lamp, etc. yourself. In most dorms, there will not be access to a kitchen or even a fridge, so it will be mandatory to buy the meal plan. The food is okay but pretty expensive. However, it saves one a lot of time not to have to get groceries, cook, or clean.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
Even though on-campus dorms were very plain, extremely overpriced, and you had to share a room, I still recommend living on campus. It was a big part of the American college experience and easy and convenient. 
OBS: even though you apply for on-campus housing there is not guarantee that you will get it. First, I wasn't granted on-campus housing so I had to spend a lot of time looking for rooms/apartments off-campus. That was quite complicated. However, a few weeks before traveling to the US, BC announced they had some more dorm rooms available, and I was able to get one there. If you apply for dorms, and you don't get one in the first round, I recommend to keep asking them for availability. They will most likely find some extra spots later on, and if you stay in the loop, you might get lucky.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was just very different from my home university. It took me a while to figure it out. When you apply for classes in the spring upon arrival make sure to check what days and time periods, the different courses are. A lot of the courses, I wanted to take were at the same time, so I had to make quite a few adjustments.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: In January, when you create your formal application for Boston College, they ask you to list ten courses you're interested in. They have an online catalogue. You only have to take 4-5 courses but they cannot guarantee that you will get all of your top choices. Make sure that the courses you want the most do not overlap. In the spring, when you become accepted to the university and get your student account, you can see what courses they have put you in. You will still be able to make adjustments. Either you can write them an email, and they can switch you to another course if the class have any spots left. Or you can wait to the add & drop period which is the first one or two weeks of classes. Here you can try out different courses and make adjustments to your schedule. Sometimes the professors can overrule the initial student availability in their class. I ended up getting all the courses I wanted to, even though it was quite a hassle during the first two weeks.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The international team explained to us how the registration worked, and the professors are responsive and helpful as well, if you want to take their class.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Some of the classes, I wanted to take, overlapped which was a shame. However, the four classes I ended up wanting (that did not overlap) I managed to get all of them.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Make sure the courses do not overlap. 
If you are statskundskaber on 5th semester - I was able to take DAK3 but they did not have EP. Instead I took Microeconomics which I had pushed from 3rd semester. They have lots of electives to choose from, and those were easy to get accepted by KU.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I really liked my classes at Boston College. I only had holdundervisning and no forelæsninger. This meant that I felt much closer to my professors (who knew everyone's name) and much more engaged. The professors were great (except for my Microeconomics prof who really lacked structure). In every class, I had papers, quizzes, midterms, a few presentations and finals. The many deadlines of course added to the work load, but I learned a lot more this semester than on my semesters at KU, simply because I had to apply the knowledge I had achieved throughout the whole semester, rather that it all came down to one single exam by the end.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I think the academic level of my courses were pretty similar to my courses at KU. In my experience, the BC classes were less critical and more practical than KU. We did not really talk about ontology and epistemology much.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The BC style of teaching was more similar to Danish gymnasium. Closer professor-student relations and more running assignments and feedback. The amount of classes and readings were about the same.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Microeconomic Theory (Økonomi 1)
Political Parties, Voters and Party Systems in Comparative Perspective (DAK3)
Globalization (valgfag)
United States Foreign Policy 1945 to Present (valgfag)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: United States Foreign Policy 1945 to Present (valgfag) was really interesting. It was sort of a history class where we learned about and discussed US foreign policy since WWII. We discussed the strategics of different paradigms and events and different presidents. The professor was great and I feel like I learned quite a lot about American foreign policy.

Housing DKK per month *

Local transportation DKK per month *
Food DKK per month *
Personal spending DKK per month *

Other fees DKK per month *
What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer:
We had to pay a Campus Infirmary Fee on $303 when we came, in addition to the Health care. 
Gym membership on campus was $180. 
Athletic Gold Pass (to watch all the BC sports games) was $150.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Dorm room and meal plan was more expensive than I had expected. I should have known this earlier had I made better research. Living off-campus in an apartment was typically just as expensive - if not more. Of course they would have the opportunity to cook for themselves, but even groceries in Boston are quite expensive. In general, it's an expensive city to live in.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
There were all the sports and clubs that one could dream of. They had a fair in the beginning of the semester where one could talk to members of all the clubs. This could be cooking club, music clubs, film clubs, acapella clubs, various volunteering clubs, academic clubs, networking clubs. Basically everything. 
The recreational center (the gym) was amazing. They had everything - tennis courts, basketball courts, squash, swimming pool, indoor running track, climbing wall, as well as all kinds of machines and gears. They also had many different sports teams. It was hard to qualify for the competing teams, but they also had intramural teams where you could form your own team and compete against other amateur BC teams in volleyball, soccer, basketball etc.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Definitely get a gym membership. 
If you are interested in politics, I can recommend Model of United Nations. We had the chance to go to conferences at Boston University and Georgetown in Washington D.C. They participate in different conferences every semester. 
The music listeners society was fun too.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
In the fall break, we rented cars and drove to Arcadia National Park in Maine. We stayed in an Airbnb for 3 nights. The nature and hikes were absolutely amazing. 
New York City - 4.5 hours away by bus. So much to see and do!!
In late November there's Thanksgiving break. I had classes off from Wednesday to Friday (and the weekend ofc). Some had the whole week off. This is a great chance to go on a trip. I went to Charleston, SC to spend Thanksgiving with some American friends. Other exchange students went on trips to NY, Nashville, DC, Puerto Rico, Cali etc. 
I also recommend to get the most out of Boston. 
- Watch a Celtics (basketball), Bruins (ice hockey) or Red Sox (baseball) game. 
- Kayak or SUB at Charles River Esplanada in the summer or just to for a walk there all year round. 
- Check out galleries, markets and vintage shops in SoWa. 
- Walk around Beacon Hill during halloween. They'll even let you trick and treat lol. 
- Go line dancing or sing live band karaoke at Nashville bar (on Thursdays). 
- Go visit cute shops and cafes or the old movie theater in Coolidge Corner. 
- Have a drink at a speakeasy bar or rooftop bar. (maybe Yovenne's or Lookout)
- Shop and eat at Newbury Street! 
- Check out Harvard and the botanic garden in Cambridge 
- Go to Revere Beach (summer time) 
- Eat great food and listen to jazz or blues at Beehive in South End. 
- Downtown: visit Public Garden, Boston Public Library, Brattle Bookshop and Isabell Gardener museum

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: I think it was very easy to adjust. We know so much about American culture and college life from movies and medias so there's hardly much of a culture shock. College students in the US are very young (18-21) compared to Danes. There were grad students too but I didn't see them much.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: You will be introduced to the other exchange students immediately. If you live on-campus you will most likely also live in the same buildings. It's a very easy and natural group to get acquainted with. If you want to socialize with American students you have to make a little more effort. Joining clubs and societies is definitely a good way to do it. Also don't be hesitant to talk to students in your class. A lot of BC students go on exchange themselves and will most likely be quite eager to talk to you. You can also sign up for the buddy program and get a local student body who has been on exchange themselves. I also talked to many Americans who were a bit older (23-30) when I went out to the city. On bars or even just on the train ride.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer:
- That they try to make money off of you any chance they get 
- Paying tips 
- People saying "how are you" instead of just "hi" when they pass you, not expecting to engage in conversation
- American youth (especially girls) being a bit superficial: telling you they love you without really knowing you. Making plans with you but never showing up or canceling last minute. (this ofc does not happen all the time but I had quite a few of these encounters).

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The hospitality! Americans can be extremely welcoming, warm and generous when they want to. If you would like to try and celebrate Thanksgiving with Americans for instance, you could easily get invited by fellow students or even faculty.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
- Be aware it's gonna be very expensive. 
- Live on campus! (unless you really can't stand the thought of having a roommate) 
- Participate in sports games, clubs and societies and all of the events, the student organizations arrange. Boston College has such a rich and vibrant campus culture that you'll never experience in DK!

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Boston College is in the suburbs - not in the city. It takes about 20-25 minutes to reach downtown Boston by car. There're plenty Uber and Lyft cars. They also have fairly good public transportation (in American standards) and there is a T-stop near campus. However, the T is very slow, and It can take almost an hour reaching the city. Also they stop running after 1 AM or so, which means you'll have to get an Uber home if you stay out later on a night out. Everything closes at 2 AM anyways,

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer:
Feeling like I was at højskole but on university level in the US. Living on-campus really feels like living on a højskole in many ways. Not having to worry about anything outside the BC bubble. It was very un-stressful. 
It was also very rewarding to finally feel like a good student. At home I had a tendency to skip a lot of classes and readings, but there I felt much more motivated to participate in class.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer:
I don't tend to get home sick but of course you'll miss friends and family and your way of living at home. 
I honestly think my greatest challenge was everything being so expensive.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
